why_this_tool: Kubernetes is the one tool where the lesson's image, Deployment, Job and resource primitives can all be practised together on a free local cluster.
alternatives: HashiCorp Nomad is a simpler single-binary scheduler with a much smaller ML ecosystem, Docker Compose or Docker Swarm run containers without a reconciling control plane that suits batch and GPU workloads, managed cloud ML platforms hide the cluster but cannot run on a laptop, and Slurm schedules batch training well but has no native model for long-running services.

setup.do: Install a container engine, the kubectl command line tool and a local cluster tool such as minikube or kind, then start a single-node cluster.
setup.done_when: kubectl reports one node in Ready state and the client and server versions print without error.

source.title: List All Container Images Running in a Cluster | Kubernetes

setup.why: Every later step needs a running cluster and a configured kubectl. A local cluster costs nothing and needs no GPU.

setup.do: Check which container runtime your local node uses by reading the wide node listing.
setup.done_when: The node listing shows a container runtime column with a runtime name and version.

source.title: Find Out What Container Runtime is Used on a Node | Kubernetes

verified.section_found: Find out the container runtime used on a Node

setup.why: Images you build with Docker are run by containerd or another runtime inside the node. Knowing which one explains later image loading and pull behaviour.

steps.do: Run the first Kubernetes Basics modules on your local cluster: create the cluster, deploy the sample app and explore it.
steps.done_when: The sample app runs as a Pod and you can see its logs and description with kubectl.
steps.why: This is the shortest guided path from nothing to a running workload. It gives you the kubectl verbs used in every later step.

steps.do: Create a Deployment for a small CPU model server with three replicas, then delete one Pod and watch the cluster replace it.
steps.done_when: The Deployment shows three of three replicas ready again within seconds of the Pod being deleted.
steps.why: This shows the cluster model and desired state in action: you declare a replica count and the controller keeps it true. Inference services depend on this behaviour.

steps.do: Run a rolling update of the model server Deployment to a new image tag, check the rollout history, then roll back to the previous revision.
steps.done_when: Rollout history lists at least two revisions and the running Pods use the earlier image again.

verified.section_found: Rolling Back to a Previous Revision

steps.why: Shipping a new model version and reverting a bad one is the daily Deployment workflow for model servers. Rollout history is the record you compare revisions against.

steps.do: Write CPU and memory requests and limits into the model server container spec and apply the change.
steps.done_when: Describing the Pod shows the requests and limits you set, and describing the node shows them counted in allocated resources.

source.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers | Kubernetes

steps.why: Requests drive scheduling and limits cap usage. Without them, ML workloads on shared nodes starve each other.

steps.do: Run a training script as a run-to-completion Job with a deliberately low memory limit, watch it get killed, then raise the limit and run it again to completion.
steps.done_when: The first Job Pod shows a terminated state with an out of memory reason and the second Job reports one successful completion.

source.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers | Kubernetes

steps.why: Jobs are the shape for training and batch inference, and running out of memory is their most common failure. You need to recognise the termination reason quickly.

steps.do: Read how custom resources and custom controllers extend the built-in API, which is how training operators and batch queueing systems add their own job types.
steps.done_when: You can explain in two sentences how a training job custom resource differs from a built-in Job and what its controller does.
steps.why: The built-in Job covers single-container batch work. Distributed training and queued batch inference are modelled as custom resources reconciled by controllers, so you need this model before installing any of them.

steps.do: Create a Pod that requests a GPU-style extended resource. A real GPU needs a GPU node and a vendor device plugin, so on a laptop advertise a fake node-level extended resource on your node and request that instead.
steps.done_when: A Pod requesting the available amount runs, and a Pod requesting more than the node advertises stays Pending with a FailedScheduling event.

source.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers | Kubernetes

steps.why: GPUs are exposed as extended resources that must be requested as whole integers in limits. A fake resource reproduces the same scheduling behaviour without hardware.

steps.do: Install kube-state-metrics in the local cluster and query its metrics to compare desired and available replicas for your Deployment and the status of your Jobs.
steps.done_when: A metrics query returns replica and Job status values that match what kubectl shows for the same objects.

source.title: Metrics for Kubernetes Object States | Kubernetes

verified.section_found: Example: using metrics from kube-state-metrics to query the cluster state

steps.why: Object state metrics persist what the cluster believes about your workloads. They let you compare declared state against actual state over time rather than by eye.

steps.do: Package your model server code into a container image with an explicit version tag, load it into the local cluster and set the image pull policy so the node uses the loaded image.
steps.done_when: The Deployment runs your own image and the Pod events show the image was already present on the node, not pulled.
steps.why: The image is the unit you ship for ML code. Pull policy decides whether a node uses a cached image or contacts a registry, a frequent source of stale or missing model code.

steps.do: Start a local container registry with authentication, push your image to it, create a registry credential Secret and reference it from the Pod template.
steps.done_when: A fresh Pod pulls the image from the local registry successfully, and removing the Secret reference makes a new Pod fail with an image pull error.

verified.section_found: Creating a Secret with a Docker config

steps.why: Teams keep ML images in private registries. Registering the image and wiring pull credentials is the promote step every workload depends on.

steps.do: Reproduce the deployment from a clean cluster using manifests that pin the image by digest instead of a mutable tag, then list all images running in the cluster.
steps.done_when: After recreating the cluster and applying the manifests, the listed running image carries the same digest you pinned.
steps.why: A digest fixes exactly which bytes run, so a training or serving run can be repeated later or in CI. Listing running images verifies nothing drifted.

steps.do: Configure a multi-node local cluster as a production-like setup: verify that dynamic resource allocation is enabled and create a DeviceClass. Real devices need GPU nodes and a vendor driver, so on a laptop stop at the DeviceClass or use an example driver.
steps.done_when: The resource API group is listed by the cluster and your DeviceClass appears when you list device classes.

source.title: Set Up DRA in a Cluster | Kubernetes

steps.why: Production ML clusters separate node pools and hand out accelerators through device classes and drivers. Verifying the API and creating the class is the part you can rehearse locally.
